<note>The title <term>Asis Rimmonim</term> (Pomegranate Juice) refers to a classic 16th-century work of Jewish mysticism by Moses ben Jacob Cordovero. It is an abridged version of his larger encyclopedic work, *Pardes Rimmonim* (Orchard of Pomegranates). The Latin signature "Almotto" likely belongs to a later owner or a government censor who inspected the book for prohibited content.</note>

# Second Discourse
## On the Explanation of the Secret of Impregnation
<note>original: "סוד העיבור" (Sod ha-Ibur). In Kabbalah, this refers to the "impregnation" or attachment of a righteous soul to a living person to assist them in their spiritual tasks.</note>

->On the explanation of the matter as we have received it, man from the mouth of man, until our teacher Moses, peace be upon him<-

(And behold, some say that this secret is a very great and exalted secret, and it should not be revealed except to the modest among Israel). And I, the writer, have seen the words of the sages of this generation, and each one of them states his own opinion and reasoning in this matter; and each one of them brings proof for his words from the verses, from the <term>Gemara</term> <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary.</note>, and from the <term>Midrashim</term> <note>Ancient rabbinic interpretations and homilies on the Hebrew Bible.</note>. And all their words are "the words of the living God," <note>original: "דברי אלהים חיים" (Divrei Elohim Hayyim). A traditional phrase indicating that even conflicting religious opinions can contain divine truth.</note> except that each and every one of them speaks according to his own perception and according to what his hand has reached.

And I, the least among thousands, have come to write the words of the ancients, of blessed memory, who were ordained one by another, man from the mouth of man, until our teacher Moses, peace be upon him. And I saw that their words are the correct and true ones, and all their words are words of <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>In this context, the word literally means "received tradition," referring to a chain of transmission.</note>. Truly, this is a matter of the <term>intellect<note>Hebrew: *sechel*; referring here to the human faculty of reason and logical understanding.</note>, and it is agreed upon by all those who possess intellect; indeed, anyone who denies this is excluded from the company of enlightened men. <meta>This page transitions from a discussion on the nature of Divine forgiveness to a systematic categorization of spiritual virtues. It establishes a hierarchy of character traits based on classical Rabbinic sources.</meta>

An explanation of the phrase **"And in Your compassion toward us..."** <note>original: "ובחמלתך עלינו" (u-v'chemlatcha aleinu); a phrase likely from a liturgical prayer or commentary</note> and so on. The meaning is that a king of flesh and blood—when a person transgresses his commands and becomes liable for death—if the king wishes to forgive him and have pity on him, he may commute the death sentence. However, he will not restore the person to his former status that he held before he sinned. If he was a minister, the king will not restore him to his ministry; if he was an administrator, he will not restore him to his administration. But the Holy One, Blessed be He, is not like this. Rather, when a person returns in repentance, God has pity on him and restores him to his former status. Even if he was a perfectly righteous man before he sinned, he returns to his former righteousness. This is what is meant by saying, **"And in Your compassion toward us"**—meaning, the compassion You show us is a great compassion, for You restore us to our original standing. This is also what is meant by the phrase **"And You accepted us with favor,"** meaning just as we were before we sinned, when we were desired before You, so now after repentance we are desired before You. This is "And You accepted us with favor." This is also what the scripture says: "I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely" <note>Hosea 14:5</note> and so on. The meaning is: after I heal their backsliding, I will return to loving them freely, just as I loved them before they sinned. This is the meaning of "And in Your compassion toward us and You accepted us with favor."

# The Sixth Gate <margin>Explaining the definitions of the Pious, the Humble, the God-fearing, the Righteous, the Upright, the Sincere, and the Holy</margin>

It has already been explained in the *Book of Knowledge* <note>original: "Sefer HaMada," the first volume of Maimonides' code of law, which deals with basic beliefs and character traits</note> that these names are all used to describe degrees of excellence and perfection, and each one of them is higher than the other. Here, the **Pious** <term>Hasid: one who acts with loving-kindness beyond the strict requirements of the law</term> is higher than all of them, and the **Humble** <term>Anav: one who possesses true humility</term> is below him, and the **God-fearing** <term>Yere Shamayim</term> is below the Humble, and the **Righteous** <term>Tzaddik</term> is below the God-fearing, and the **Upright** <term>Yashar</term> is below the Righteous, and the **Sincere** <term>Tamim: also translated as "wholehearted" or "simple" in faith</term> is below the Upright. However, the **Holy** <term>Kadosh</term> is higher than all of them, even the Pious. This is what our Sages, of blessed memory, said in the final chapter of the tractate *Avodah Zarah* <note>original: "Foreign Worship," a volume of the Talmud</note>: "Torah leads to watchfulness; watchfulness leads to alacrity; alacrity leads to cleanliness; cleanliness leads to abstinence; abstinence leads to purity; purity leads to piety; piety leads to humility; humility leads to fear of sin; fear of sin leads to holiness; holiness leads to the Holy Spirit" and so on. Thus, the order of these levels is one above the other, and Holiness is the highest of all, for it leads to the Holy Spirit. Now, we shall explain each and every one of them.

<column-break/>

**The First Level is the level of the Sincere.** This means that one should be sincere in his actions with God, may He be blessed, and should not investigate or question the attributes of the Holy One, Blessed be He. Rather, whatever comes upon him, he should receive it with love. This is what the scripture means: "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 18:13</note>. Our Sages, of blessed memory, said: "Walk with Him in sincerity and do not investigate His attributes." This is also what King David, peace be upon him, said: "As for me, I walked in my integrity" <note>Psalms 26:11</note>. Our Sages said in the *Midrash on Psalms*: What is meant by "I walked in my integrity"? David said before the Holy One, Blessed be He: "Master of the Universe, when You brought suffering upon me, I did not question Your attributes, but rather I accepted them with love." This is "I walked in my integrity." Similarly, he says in Psalms: "A Psalm of David: The Lord is my light and my salvation... Seek My face; Your face, O Lord, I will seek. Hide not Your face from me..." and afterward it says, "Had I not believed to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living. Hope in the Lord; be strong and let your heart take courage, and hope in the Lord" <note>Psalms 27</note>. Our Sages interpreted this in the *Midrash on Psalms*: What is the meaning of "Had I not believed"? David said before the Holy One, Blessed be He: "Master of the Universe, I know that You pay a good reward to the righteous in the time to come, but I do not know if I have a portion with them or not; perhaps sin will cause me to lose it." This is "Had I not believed to see the goodness of the Lord." Afterward, he said, "Hope in the Lord; be strong and let your heart take courage"—meaning, even though you fear that sin may disqualify you, nevertheless, hope in the Lord and do not despair of mercy. This is the level of the Sincere man who does not question the attributes of the Holy One, Blessed be He.

**The Second Level is the level of the Upright.** This is one who performs his deeds with integrity, does not twist his ways, and does not flatter any person. Rather, all his words are in truth and integrity. This is what the scripture says: "The ways of the Lord are upright; the righteous walk in them, but the rebellious stumble in them" <note>Hosea 14:10</note>. And it says: "Sing for joy, O righteous, in the Lord; praise is becoming to the upright" <note>Psalms 33:1</note>. And it says: "Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart" <note>Psalms 97:11</note>. This level is very great, and a person must conduct himself by it.

**The Third Level is the level of the Righteous.** This is one whose every action is done with justice. He commits no wrong—neither in matters of money, nor in speech, nor in anything else. Rather, everything is with justice and integrity. This is what the scripture says: "The Lord is righteous in all His ways, and pious in all His works" <note>Psalms 145:17</note>. And it says: "Justice, justice shall you pursue, that you may live and inherit the land" <note>Deuteronomy 16:20</note>. This level is very great, and a person must be very careful in it. Anyone who is righteous in his deeds is loved by the Holy One, Blessed be He. This is what the scripture says: "The Lord tests the righteous" and "For the Lord is righteous, He loves righteousness; the upright shall behold His face" <note>Psalms 11:5, 11:7</note>.

**The Fourth Level is the level of the God-fearing.** This is one who fears God, may He be blessed, at all times, does not transgress His commandments, and fears punishment. This level is very great, and this is what the scripture says: "The Lord your God you shall fear, and Him you shall serve" <note>Deuteronomy 6:13</note>. And it says: "The end of the matter, all having been heard: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man" <note>Ecclesiastes 12:13</note>. This level is the foundation for all levels, and one who lacks the fear of Heaven possesses none of these levels. This is what our Sages, of blessed memory, said: "Anyone who possesses Torah but lacks the fear of Heaven is like a treasurer who was given the keys to the inner chambers, but the keys to the outer gates were not given to him—how then shall he enter?"

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the ethical discussion of divine forgiveness into deep Kabbalistic metaphysics. It explores the Lurianic concept of "Adam Kadmon" (Primordial Man) and how the infinite Divine Light organizes itself into the Ten Sefirot to interact with the world.</meta>

<margin>
And this is the secret of the **Living God** <note>original: *Elohim Chayim*</note> and **King of the Universe, God Almighty** <note>original: *El Shaddai*</note>.
</margin>

<image-desc>A triangular diagram pointing downwards, divided into three horizontal sections. Hebrew letters representing divine names and attributes are inscribed within the sections and around the perimeter of the triangle. Lines extend from the vertices, suggesting the flow of divine emanation.</image-desc>

And behold, as He <note>the Infinite Creator</note> emanates and shines within these **Ten Sefirot** <term>Sefirot: the ten divine attributes or channels through which God interacts with the universe</term> mentioned previously—which are like vessels containing the soul that clothes itself within them—He spreads out through them, clothes Himself in them, and unites with them. Through them, He performs His actions and supervises His world. 

In this aspect, He is called by different names according to the changes in His actions and the changes in the "vessels" <note>the Sefirot</note>. For behold, in the aspect of **Kindness** <note>original: *Chesed*</note>, He is called by the name **El**; in the aspect of **Strength** <note>original: *Gevurah*—often associated with judgment</note>, He is called **Elohim**; and in the aspect of **Compassion** <note>original: *Rachamim*</note>, He is called **YHVH**. The same applies to the rest of the Sefirot, as is known.

In this aspect, He is called by the name **Adam** <note>Man</note>, following the analogy of the soul that clothes itself in the limbs of the body and acts through them. Just as the soul’s functions change according to the organs—seeing through the eye, hearing through the ear, and acting through the hand—so too is the **Emanator, Blessed be He**, called "Adam" in this context. This is the secret behind the verse, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness" <note>Genesis 1:26</note>. Just as the lower human being possesses 248 limbs and 365 sinews <note>a traditional Rabbinic count of the body's structure</note> which all serve as vessels for the soul to act through, so too Above there are Ten Sefirot which serve as vessels for the Emanator, Blessed be He; He clothes Himself in them and performs His works through them.

Behold, these Ten Sefirot are divided into five **Partzufim** <term>Partzufim: "Personas" or "Divine Faces," which are complex configurations of the Sefirot</term>, which are: **The Long Face** <note>original: *Arich Anpin*</note>, **Father** <note>original: *Abba*</note>, **Mother** <note>original: *Imma*</note>, **The Small Face** <note>original: *Zeir Anpin*</note>, and **His Female** <note>original: *Nukvah*</note>. These correspond to the five parts of the Divine Name <note>the four letters of the Tetragrammaton plus the "tip" of the first letter</note> and to the five levels of the soul, which are: **Nefesh** <note>Life-force</note>, **Ruach** <note>Spirit</note>, **Neshama** <note>Breath/Soul</note>, **Chaya** <note>Living Essence</note>, and **Yechida** <note>Singular Essence</note>. Each of these five "Faces" contains its own ten Sefirot, and each Sefirah within them is composed of another ten, infinitely. All of this refers to the aspect of the "vessels" and the "soul" <note>the Divine light</note> that clothes itself in them, as mentioned.

<column-break/>

This is the secret of what our Sages of blessed memory said in the Midrash <note>Genesis Rabbah</note> regarding the verse: "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God He created him." Rabbi Levi said in the name of Rabbi Chama bar Chanina: "As it were, He created him in His own likeness, as it is written: 'In the image of God He created him.'" 

The matter is this: just as the Emanator, Blessed be He, created the lower man in His image and likeness, it means He did so in the aspect of the Ten Sefirot, which are the aspect of the **Supernal Man** <note>original: *Adam HaElyon*</note> mentioned before. This is the secret of "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness." In this aspect, the Emanator, Blessed be He, is called by the name **Adam**, and this is the secret of the verse: "And upon the likeness of the throne was a likeness as the appearance of a **man** above upon it" <note>Ezekiel 1:26</note>. This is the secret of the **Man of Emanation** <note>original: *Adam d'Atzilut*</note>, which is the Emanator, Blessed be He, clothing Himself in the Ten Sefirot of the world of Emanation.

In this aspect, He is called by the Name **YHVH** in its "filled" form <note>a Kabbalistic method of spelling out the names of the letters</note> using the vowel *Aleph*, which equals the numerical value <note>Gematria</note> of 45 <note>the letters Yud-He-Vav-He spelled out as Y-V-D, H-A, V-A-V, H-A equal 45</note>. This is the same numerical value as the word **Adam** <note>A=1, D=4, M=40</note>. This is the secret of what is said in the *Tikunim* <note>Tikunei Zohar</note> on page 107b, which states: "The Man of Emanation <note>Atzilut</note> is not like the Man of Creation <note>Briyah</note>, who is the angel **Metatron**; rather, the Man of Emanation is the Name YHVH, which is the form of all things," and so on; see there.

<margin>
<unclear>A brief note in a cramped hand, likely a citation or a cross-reference to another Kabbalistic work</unclear>
</margin>

Now, you must know that these Ten Sefirot of Emanation, which are the aspect of the Supernal Man, were emanated in two aspects: **Circles** and **Uprightness** <note>original: *Igulim* and *Yosher*</note>. The matter is thus: at first, the Emanator, Blessed be He, emanated the Ten Sefirot in the aspect of **Circles**, one inside the other like the layers of an onion. These are ten spheres, one within the other, and they are called the "Ten Sefirot of Circles." 

Afterward, He emanated them in the aspect of **Uprightness**, which consists of three lines: right, left, and middle. These are called the "Ten Sefirot of Uprightness," and they clothe themselves within the Circles. This aspect of Uprightness is the aspect of the **Supernal Man** mentioned previously, who possesses 248 limbs and 365 sinews, exactly in the likeness of the lower human being.

And how can it be said that God did not know from the beginning those who would believe and those who would not? Some argue that everything is purely the result of the action of human free will <note>Syriac: *ḥerutha*, meaning freedom or agency</note>, and only after humans act are they known to God. If this were true, then prophecy would be worth nothing. Prophecy exists only because God knows in advance what is destined to happen and makes it known to us through the prophets.

If it were not so, and if God did not know what was to come, how could He have said through the prophet: *Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel* <note>A reference to Isaiah 7:14, traditionally interpreted by Christians as a prophecy of the birth of Jesus</note>? Behold, it is proper that we investigate this matter with a broad inquiry and examine the roots of the Torah and the words of our Sages of blessed memory <note>Hebrew: *Raza"l*, an acronym for 'Our Sages of Blessed Memory,' referring to the classical rabbis of the Talmud</note>, as well as what true contemplation necessitates. Behold, we shall explain here in this matter that which will suffice for what we are currently explaining.

We say that it has already been explained in this place with a complete explanation that God, may He be exalted, knows existing things according to the reality they possess. Behold, the existence of things is of two types: either a limited and ordered existence, or a possible existence from the side of the choice that was given to man. And behold, God, may He be exalted, knows ordered and limited things according to the order and limitation they possess. However, as for possible things, behold, God, may He be exalted, knows them from the side of their being possible. This is because He knows that it is possible for this thing to be, and possible for it not to be. But as for which of the two extremes will actually occur, He, may He be exalted, does not know it from the side of it being ordered and limited, for it has no order or limitation from the side of it being possible. If He knew it from the side of it being limited <note>Meaning 'determined' or 'predestined'</note>, that thing would be a necessity and would not be possible. This is something that has already been explained with a complete explanation in its proper place.

And since the matter is so, behold, God, may He be exalted, knows possible things from the side of their being possible. And behold, from the side of their being possible, they are unknown as to which of the two extremes will actually occur. However, God, may He be exalted, knows them from the side of their being possible—meaning to say, He knows that it is possible for them to be and possible for them not to be.

And behold, when one of the extremes actually occurs, then God, may He be exalted, knows it then from the side of its existing in actuality. However, before then, He did not know it from the side of its existing in actuality, because it did not yet exist in actuality. And behold, knowledge of a thing according to what it is does not necessitate a change in the Knower. This is because knowledge is the apprehension of a thing as it is. Behold, when the thing was possible, its apprehension as it is was an apprehension from the side of it being possible. And when it exists in actuality, its apprehension as it is is an apprehension from the side of it existing in actuality. This does not necessitate a change in the knowledge, but it necessitates a change in the *known* <note>The author argues that God's mind doesn't change; only the status of the event in the world changes from 'potential' to 'actual'</note>. This is because the knowledge is one, being the apprehension of the thing as it is. And behold, when the "known" changes, its apprehension as it is will necessarily change. This is not a change in the knowledge from its own side, but a change from the side of the object known.

And when it exists in actuality, its apprehension as it is is an apprehension from the side of it existing in actuality. This does not necessitate a change in the knowledge, but it necessitates a change in the known. This is because the knowledge is one, being the apprehension of the thing as it is. And behold, when the "known" changes, its apprehension as it is will necessarily change. This is not a change in the knowledge from its own side, but a change from the side of the object known. And behold, this matter is very clear to whoever has examined our words in this place. And after this has been explained, behold...

<meta>This page appears to be a study of the laws of ritual slaughter (Shechitah) and animal anatomy, specifically focusing on "supernumerary" (extra) organs. ### On the Laws of Anatomical Defects

<margin>
Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, wrote in the chapter titled "These are the Defects" <note>Original: *Elu Terefot*, a chapter in the Talmudic tractate Chullin</note>: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rav that any extra part is [forbidden], but Rav Ashi said that any part not found in the "place of the cut" <note>Referring to the specific anatomical regions where the lungs are divided</note> is not considered a forbidden extra, and is thus fit for consumption.
</margin>

<margin>
**Maimonides** <note>The Rambam, 1138–1204</note>, of blessed memory, wrote in the sixth chapter of the *Laws of Ritual Slaughter*: If an extra organ is found—for example, if the animal has two lungs, two livers, two gallbladders, two spleens, two stomachs, two omasums <note>Original: *misesot*, one of the four stomach compartments</note>, or two second stomachs <note>Original: *batei cosot*, the reticulum</note>—it is considered **treifah** <note>Unfit for consumption</note>. This is based on the general rule: **Every extra part is treated as if it were missing**, and any missing organ renders the animal unfit, except for the spleen and the kidneys; if those are missing, the animal remains fit.
</margin>

<margin>
The **Tur** <note>Jacob ben Asher, c. 1269–1343</note>, of blessed memory, wrote in Section 41: **Every extra part is treated as if it were missing**, and any missing organ renders the animal unfit, except for the spleen and the kidneys; if those are missing, the animal remains fit.
</note>
</margin>

<margin>

(This parable concerns merchants who would sell merchandise in one country and purchase different merchandise in another country.)
Now, it is the custom that they sell the merchandise at a set price and buy the other merchandise at a set price. (Behold, if they sell the first merchandise at a high price <note>Literally: "in dearness"</note> and buy the second at a low price, they will profit greatly; but if they sell the first at a low price and buy the second at a high price, they will lose greatly. If they sell the first at a high price and buy the second at a high price, they will neither profit nor lose; likewise, if they sell the first at a low price and buy the second at a low price, they will neither profit nor lose.)

Now, this parable is an analogy for the soul that comes into this world <note>Hebrew: *Olam HaZeh*, referring to our physical life on earth</note> to acquire commandments <term>Mitzvot; divine deeds or obligations</term> and good deeds. This world is the "country" where the merchandise is sold, and the World to Come <note>Hebrew: *Olam HaBa*, referring to the spiritual realm or afterlife</note> is the "country" where the merchandise is bought.

(Behold, if a person "sells" his days in this world at a high price—meaning he occupies himself with the study of Torah and the performance of commandments—and "buys" the World to Come at a low price—meaning he merits the life of the World to Come—he will profit greatly. But if he sells his days at a low price—meaning he occupies himself with the vanities of this world—and buys the World to Come at a high price—meaning he does not merit the life of the World to Come—he will lose greatly.)

This parable is pleasant and acceptable to the heart. (Behold, there are several things here that must be explained very clearly.) The first point is what he said: (that they would sell merchandise in one country and buy other merchandise in another country). The first country is This World, and the second country is the World to Come. (The first merchandise consists of a person's days in this world, and the second merchandise is life in the World to Come.) The "selling" is the labor in Torah and commandments, and the "buying" is the merit of life in the World to Come.

(Behold, if a person sells his days at a high price—meaning he occupies himself extensively with Torah and commandments—he will buy the World to Come "cheaply"—meaning he will merit the life of the World to Come with ease.) But if he sells his days cheaply—meaning he occupies himself with the vanities of this world—he will buy the World to Come "dearly"—meaning he will not merit the life of the World to Come except with great difficulty. (This parable is a true analogy, and it is proper for every person to take it to heart.)

The second point is what he said: (Now, it is the custom that they sell the merchandise at a set price and buy the other merchandise at a set price). The "set price" is the time allotted to a person in this world. (If a person utilizes this time for the service of the Name, may He be blessed <note>A common Jewish substitution for the name of God</note>, he will profit greatly.) But if a person wastes this time on the vanities of this world, he will lose greatly. (The "set price" of the World to Come consists of the good deeds that a person performs in this world.) If a person increases his good deeds, he will buy the World to Come "cheaply." (But if a person diminishes his good deeds, he will buy the World to Come "dearly.")

This parable is comprehensive, covering all the affairs of man in this world and the World to Come. (It is proper for every wise person to contemplate this parable and learn from it the upright path in which to walk.) May the Name, may He be blessed, help us for the sake of His glorious name. Amen, Selah <note>A liturgical conclusion meaning "forever"</note>.

# The Eighth Gate
->Regarding the explanation of the Garment, the Amber Glow, the Brightness, and the Shells<-

Behold, we have already explained in the previous gate the matter of the <term>Garment</term><note>original: "Malbush"; refers to a spiritual protective layer or interface</note> made from the "Surrounding Lights" of the <term>Father and Mother</term><note>original: "Abba ve-Imma"; these are the high-level divine configurations representing Wisdom and Understanding</note>. We explained there that this Garment is the aspect of the <term>Amber Glow</term><note>original: "Chashmal"; a mystical term for a brilliant electrical or amber radiance, famously seen in the vision of the Prophet Ezekiel</note> which surrounds <term>The Lesser Countenance</term><note>original: "Zeir Anpin"; the divine persona that governs the emotional and ethical attributes of the universe</note>. You must know that this Garment is the aspect of "Surrounding Lights" for the Lesser Countenance, and they are the aspects of the Kindnesses and the Strengths of the Father and Mother from which this Garment is made. This Garment is the Amber Glow, and it is a very great light that surrounds the Lesser Countenance. Within this Amber Glow, there is the aspect of <term>Brightness</term><note>original: "Nogah"; a glowing light that occupies a middle ground between pure holiness and total darkness</note>, which is a very subtle light and is the aspect of the Shell known as "Nogah." This Brightness is the intermediary between the Holiness and the Impure Shells.

<margin>
<unclear>...the matter of the Amber Glow...</unclear>
</margin>

This Amber Glow is a light that surrounds the Lesser Countenance from all its sides, and it is the Garment in which the Lesser Countenance is clothed. Within this Amber Glow, there is the aspect of Brightness, which is a very subtle light and is the aspect of the Shell known as "Nogah." This Brightness is the intermediary between the Holiness and the Impure Shells. This Amber Glow is a light that surrounds the Lesser Countenance from all its sides, and it is the Garment in which the Lesser Countenance is clothed.

# The Ninth Gate
->Regarding the explanation of the Shells and the order of their attachment<-

Behold, we have already explained that the <term>Shells</term><note>original: "Klipot"; the forces of evil or impurity that "shell" the divine sparks</note> are the refuse of the lights that emerged during the <term>Shattering of the Vessels</term><note>original: "Shevirat Ha-Kelim"; a cosmic crisis where the divine vessels could not contain the light and broke, leading to the creation of the lower worlds</note>. These Shells are absolute evil and contain no spark of holiness at all. These Shells are the aspect of the Three Impure Shells called: "Storm Wind," "Great Cloud," and "Flashing Fire"<note>These names are taken from the vision of Ezekiel 1:4 and represent the core levels of the demonic realm</note>. These Shells are the dwelling of the <term>Extraneous Ones</term><note>original: "Chitzonim"; the demonic or parasitic forces</note> and the place where the Shells reside.

<margin>
<unclear>...the secret of the Shells...</unclear>
</margin>

You must know that these Shells have no vitality of their own at all; rather, all their life-force comes from the <term>Sparks of Holiness</term><note>original: "Nitzotzot"; fragments of divine light trapped in the physical and impure worlds</note> that fell into them during the Shattering of the Vessels. These Sparks are the vitality of the Shells, and without them, the Shells would have no existence at all. The <term>Work of Refinement</term><note>original: "Birurim"; the spiritual process of sifting good from evil through prayer and mitzvot</note> is to extract these Sparks from within the Shells and elevate them back to the Holiness.

<margin>
<unclear>...the matter of Refinement...</unclear>
</note>

When the Sparks leave the Shells, the Shells remain without vitality and are completely nullified. This is the secret of the verse: "He will swallow up death forever"<note>original: Isaiah 25:8</note>, for when the Refinement of all the Sparks is completed, the Shells will be completely nullified and there will be no memory of them in the world. The "Nogah" Brightness is the intermediary between Holiness and the Shells, representing good and evil mixed together.

# The Torah Portion
<margin>
<unclear>And the Lord said to Moses</unclear>
</margin>

**"Behold, I make a covenant: before all your people I will do marvels, such as have not been wrought in all the earth, nor in any nation; and all the people among whom you are shall see the work of the Lord, for it is a fearful thing that I am doing with you."** <note>Exodus 34:10</note>
And the scripture says: **"If You deal thus with me, kill me, I pray You, out of hand, if I have found favor in Your sight; and let me not see my wretchedness."** <note>Numbers 11:15; Moses' plea to God during the wanderings in the desert</note>

<margin>
<unclear>In the Midrash</unclear>
</margin>
In the <term>Midrash</term><note>original: "Midrash"; an ancient rabbinic method of interpreting the Bible through stories and homilies</note>, Rabbi Levi said: At the hour that the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moses, "Behold, I make a covenant," Moses said before Him: "Master of the Universe! Is everything You are destined to give me being given as a gift?" The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to him: "No, rather I make a covenant." Moses said before Him: "Master of the Universe, if You make a covenant, why do You say to me, 'kill me, I pray You, out of hand'?" The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to him: "Moses, by your life, I have sworn an oath to you that I will not leave you until I show you everything that I created during the six days of Creation."

<margin>
<unclear>Verse</unclear>
</margin>
**"Observe that which I command you this day: behold, I drive out before you the Amorite, and the Canaanite, and the Hittite, and the Perizzite, and the Hivite, and the Jebusite. Take heed to yourself, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land where you are going, lest it be for a snare in the midst of you. But you shall break down their altars, and dash in pieces their pillars, and you shall cut down their Asherim. For you shall bow down to no other god; for the Lord, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God."** <note>Exodus 34:11-14; commandments regarding the conquest of Canaan and the rejection of idolatry</note>

<margin>
<unclear>Commentary</unclear>
</margin>
<term>Rashi</term><note>original: "Rashi"; the acronym for Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator</note>, of blessed memory, explained: **"Take heed to yourself, lest you make a covenant"**—if you make a covenant with them, it will become a snare for you. **"But you shall break down their altars"**—it is a commandment upon you to shatter their altars. **"For you shall bow down to no other god"**—that you should not perform idol worship. **"For the Lord, whose name is Jealous"**—He is zealous to exact punishment from those who worship idols.

<margin>
<unclear>Further there</unclear>
</margin>
**"Lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and they go astray after their gods, and sacrifice to their gods, and one call you and you eat of his sacrifice. And you take of their daughters for your sons, and their daughters go astray after their gods, and make your sons go astray after their gods. You shall make for yourself no molten gods."** <note>Exodus 34:15-17</note>

<margin>
<unclear>Ramban</unclear>
</margin>
And the <term>Ramban</term><note>original: "Ramban"; the acronym for Rabbi Moshe ben Nahman (1194–1270), a leading Sephardic scholar and mystic</note>, of blessed memory, wrote: The reason for **"You shall make for yourself no molten gods"** is that after He warned against idolatry in general, He returned and warned against the "molten god" <note>original: "Massekhah"; cast metal statues</note> specifically. This is because it is made with great effort and extraordinary craftsmanship, and people thought it possessed more power than other types of carved idols.

<margin>
<unclear>Verse</unclear>
</margin>
**"The feast of unleavened bread shall you keep. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time appointed in the month Abib; for in the month Abib you came out from Egypt. All that opens the womb is Mine; and all your cattle that is male, the firstlings of ox and sheep. And the firstling of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb; and if you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck. All the first-born of your sons you shall redeem. And none shall appear before Me empty."** <note>Exodus 34:18-20; regarding Passover and the sanctity of the firstborn</note>

<margin>
<unclear>Midrash</unclear>
</margin>
In the Midrash, Rabbi Isaac said: Why is the section of the firstborn juxtaposed with the section of the pilgrimage festivals? To tell you that anyone who does not go up for the pilgrimage <note>The three annual festivals—Passover, Shavuot, and Sukkot—when Israelites traveled to the Temple in Jerusalem</note> is as if he worships idols; and anyone who goes up for the pilgrimage is as if he fulfills the commandment of the firstborn.

<margin>
<unclear>Verse</unclear>
</margin>
**"Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest; in plowing time and in harvest you shall rest. And you shall observe the feast of weeks, even of the first-fruits of wheat harvest, and the feast of ingathering at the turn of the year. Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord God, the God of Israel."** <note>Exodus 34:21-23; regarding the Sabbath and the three festivals</note>

<margin>
<unclear>Commentary</unclear>
</margin>
Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: **"In plowing time and in harvest you shall rest"**—why was this said? Has it not already been stated, "Six days you shall work, and on the seventh day you shall rest"? Rather, it comes to teach about the plowing of the eve of the seventh year <note>The Sabbatical year or Shemitah</note> that enters into the seventh year, and about the harvest of the seventh year that extends into the conclusion of the seventh year.

<margin>
<unclear>Further there</unclear>
</margin>
**"For I will cast out nations before you, and enlarge your borders; neither shall any man desire your land, when you go up to appear before the Lord your God three times in the year. You shall not offer the blood of My sacrifice with leavened bread; neither shall the sacrifice of the feast of the passover be left until the morning. The first of the first-fruits of your ground you shall bring to the house of the Lord your God. You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk."** <note>Exodus 34:24-26</note>

<margin>
<unclear>Midrash</unclear>
</margin>
In the Midrash, Rabbi Levi said: At the hour that the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moses, "You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk," Moses said before Him: "Master of the Universe, is there a kid in its mother's milk?" The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to him: "Moses, by your life, Israel is destined to sin with the Calf and say, 'These are your gods, O Israel,' and I will say to them: 'You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk.'" <note>The Midrash creates a wordplay or conceptual link between the Golden Calf and the prohibition of mixing meat and milk</note>

<summary>This page describes the Names and Attributes associated with the ten Sefirot (Divine Emanations) and emphasizes their fractal structure—the concept that each emanation contains all ten within itself, repeated ad infinitum.</summary>
<keywords>Sefirot, Atziluth, Ein Sof, Keter, Chokhmah, Binah, Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach, Hod, Yesod, Malkhut, Kabbalah, Emanation, Divine Will</keywords>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the structural description of the Sefirot (divine attributes) to the practical and mystical application of these concepts in human life. It contrasts the limited understanding of traditional moralists with the profound "Path of Thought," which the author views as the ultimate gateway to the Divine.</meta>

<margin>
<unclear>Annotation</unclear> on the book *The Part of Thought*
</margin>

In a similar manner, those who are called the "Masters of Character" <note>original: *Hachmei ha-Midot*, referring to ethical philosophers or moralists</note>—that is, the teachers of ethics and virtue—also found these concepts and understood them according to their own wisdom. They approached them with simple faith and the integrity of their hearts; nonetheless, they remain lost on the road, for they do not know their own judgment or the judgment of the Lord. They neither know nor understand; they walk in darkness, and all the foundations of the earth are shaken <note>A reference to Psalm 82:5, suggesting that without divine insight, the world’s moral order is unstable</note>. And behold, the Lord looks down from heaven to see if there is any who is wise, any who seeks God. But all have turned away, together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, no, not even one. Regarding this it is said: "For My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways My ways... for as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are My ways higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts" <note>original Hebrew: Isaiah 55:8-9</note>. Behold, all those thoughts and ways that are based on the sight of flesh and blood are but vanity and a striving after wind.

For only the path that the Lord has chosen is the true and straight path which will elevate a person to the highest level and to true happiness. Behold, this path is the way of the Torah and the Commandment <note>original: *Mitzvah*</note> which the Lord commanded His servant Moses to teach the Children of Israel. This is the path of life and peace; it is the way in which a man shall walk and find rest for his soul. This is the path of faith and trust in the Lord, and it is the way through which a person finds success in this world and in the World to Come. This is the path of the love and fear of the Lord, the way through which a person finds his attachment <term>Dveikut: a state of meditative "cleaving" or spiritual attachment to God</term> to the Creator, blessed be He. This is the path of service and prayer to the Lord, the way to find the Lord's mercy and kindness. This is the path of repentance and forgiveness, the way to find atonement for one's sins. This is the path of charity and kindness toward fellow creatures, the way to find the Lord’s grace. This is the path of humility and lowliness before the Lord, the way to find true spiritual height. This is the path of abstinence and holiness, the way to find purity. This is the path of wisdom and understanding in the Torah of the Lord, the way to find the light of the Lord and His salvation. This is the path of truth and integrity in all one’s actions, the way to find the Lord’s peace and blessing. All these ways are actually one single path: the Way of the Lord which He commanded us to follow. This is the path of life and good, which a person should choose so that he and his descendants may live. This is the path of blessing and success, the way to find all the heart’s good desires. This is the path of joy and rejoicing in the Lord, the way to find the Lord’s delight and sweetness. This is the path of rest and the inheritance of the Lord, the way to find eternal rest.

<column-break/>

<margin>
The <unclear>Secret</unclear> of Thought
</margin>

But the specific path that the Lord has chosen is the Path of Thought and the Intention of the heart and soul; this is the way through which a person finds the "secret of the Lord for those who fear Him, and His covenant to make them know it" <note>original Hebrew: Psalm 25:14</note>. This is the path of attachment and contemplation of the greatness of the Lord and His wonders, the way to find the knowledge and perception of God. This is the path of self-nullification <term>Bitul: the mystical process of negating the ego to become a vessel for divine light</term> and inclusion within the light and radiance of the Lord; it is the way a person finds the life of the World to Come while still alive in this world. This is the path of prophecy and the Holy Spirit, the way to find the word of the Lord and His counsel. This is the path of wonders and miracles, the way to find the Lord’s might and salvation. This is the path of perfection and integrity, the way to find the Lord’s will and what He seeks. This is the path of unity and oneness <note>original: *Yichud*, referring to the declaration of God’s absolute unity</note>, the way to find that "the Lord is one and His name is one." This is the path of light and life, the way to find the "light of the King's countenance." This is the path of the holy and the Sanctuary, the way to find the indwelling of the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah: the feminine, immanent aspect of God that dwells within the world</term> inside oneself. This is the path of redemption and ransom, the way to find the redemption of one's soul and the redemption of Israel. This is the path of the Messiah and the Kingdom, the way to find the Lord's kingship over all the earth. This is the path of resurrection and eternity, the way to find the resurrection of the dead and eternal life.

All these ways are one single path: the path of Pure and Lucid Thought, which is the beginning of all and the end of all. Thought is the spiritual power within man, the force by which a person connects to his Creator. Thought is the vessel through which a person receives the divine flow <note>original: *Shefa*, the emanation of divine energy</note> and blessing. Thought is the key that opens the gates of heaven. Thought is the Chariot <note>original: *Merkavah*, a reference to Ezekiel’s vision of the divine throne-chariot</note> upon which a person rides to ascend to the Lord. Thought is the altar upon which a person offers his soul to the Lord. Thought is the sacrifice that the Lord desires from us. Thought is the true prayer that ascends before the Throne of Glory. Thought is the "service of the heart," which is the essence of all worship. Thought is the greatest commandment of all the commandments. Thought is the entire Torah "on one foot" <note>A reference to the famous story of the sage Hillel, who summarized the Torah while standing on one leg</note>. Thought is everything, and there is nothing outside of it. Thought is the Lord, and the Lord is Thought.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the Sephirot (divine emanations), moving from the upper triad of the mind (Crown, Wisdom, Understanding) to the emotive attributes that govern the created world. The previous page listed divine names associated with each Sephirah; this page provides the theological descriptions and associations for the fourth, fifth, and sixth spheres.</meta>

## The Fourth Sephirah is that which is called *Chesed* [Loving-kindness] and Love, and sometimes it is called *Gedulah* [Greatness]
<margin>These three names—Loving-kindness, Greatness, and Love—correspond to the three Patriarchs: Loving-kindness to Abraham, Greatness to Isaac, and Love to Jacob.</margin>
Because it is the beginning of the <term>Building<note>original: *Binyan*. In Kabbalah, this refers to the lower seven Sephirot that "build" or structure our manifest reality.</note></term> and it is the attribute of the First Day [of Creation], and it is the attribute of Abraham our father, peace be upon him. It is the Right Side among all the attributes, and it receives from <term>Wisdom<note>original: *Chokhmah*</note></term> and flows to all the attributes, and it guides the world with loving-kindness and mercy. It is called Greatness because it is greater than all the attributes, and it receives from the <term>Crown<note>original: *Keter*</note></term> and it guides the world with loving-kindness and mercy. It is called Greatness because it is greater than all the attributes, and it receives from the Crown and it guides the world with loving-kindness and mercy. It is called Greatness because it is greater than all the attributes, and it receives from the Crown and it guides the world with loving-kindness and mercy.

## The Fifth Sephirah is that which is called *Pachad* [Fear], *Gevurah* [Strength], and *Din* [Judgment], and sometimes it is called *Elohim*
<margin>Strength corresponds to Isaac.</margin>
From the right side <note>The text here says "right side," though kabbalistically Strength/Judgment is always the Left Side. This may be a scribal error or refers to a specific mystical movement, as the text immediately clarifies it is the "Left Side" in the next phrase.</note> and it is the attribute of Isaac our father, peace be upon him. It is the Left Side among all the attributes, and it receives from <term>Understanding<note>original: *Binah*</note></term> and flows to all the attributes, and it guides the world with judgment and mercy. It is called Strength because it overpowers <note>The Hebrew *Gevurah* (Strength) shares a root with *Goveret* (overpowering/prevailing).</note> all the attributes, and it receives from the Crown and it guides the world with judgment and mercy. It is called Strength because it overpowers all the attributes, and it receives from the Crown and it guides the world with judgment and mercy. It is called Strength because it overpowers all the attributes, and it receives from the Crown and it guides the world with judgment and mercy.

## The Sixth Sephirah is that which is called *Tiferet* [Beauty], Truth, and Mercy, and sometimes it is called *Shalom* [Peace]
<margin>Beauty corresponds to Jacob.</margin>
<margin>And these are the Seven Days of the Building, corresponding to the seven days of Creation.</margin>
And it is the attribute of Jacob our father, peace be upon him. It is the Body <note>In the metaphorical "Divine Body," *Tiferet* represents the torso or heart, balancing the two arms of Loving-kindness and Strength.</note> among all the attributes, and it receives from Loving-kindness and from Strength, and it guides the world with mercy. It is called Beauty because it prides itself <note>A wordplay on the root *P-A-R*, meaning both beauty and glorification/pride.</note> over all the attributes, and it receives from the Crown and it guides the world with mercy. It is called Beauty because it prides itself over all the attributes, and it receives from the Crown and it guides the world with mercy. It is called Beauty because it prides itself over all the attributes, and it receives from the Crown and it guides the world with mercy.

### The Tree of the Sephirot
*The following page contains a sacred diagram of the Tree of Life. Ten circles represent the divine attributes, interconnected by twenty-two paths. In a rare display of three-dimensional book-making, the scribe has attached small squares of parchment over the circles. Through these, tufts of yellow silk thread have been knotted, likely to serve as tactile mnemonic devices or to signify the "flow" of divine light through the nodes of the Crown, Wisdom, Understanding, Loving-kindness, Strength, Beauty, Eternity, Splendor, and Foundation.*

<meta>This page transitions from the legal discussions of Sabbath carrying (folio 23) to a much earlier section of the manuscript (folio 2a). ### The Thirteenth Gate
->Regarding the explanation of the seventh rule of the <term>principles</term> <note>Hebrew: middot; refers to the thirteen hermeneutic rules used in Rabbinic logic to interpret the Torah</note> by which the Torah is interpreted<-

This rule consists of two matters. The first is: "Anything that was included in a <term>general rule</term> <note>Hebrew: klal</note> but was singled out <note>literally "went out" from the general rule</note> to teach something, was not singled out to teach about itself alone, but was singled out to teach about the whole general rule." The second is: "Anything that was included in a general rule but was singled out to present another argument that is consistent with its context, was singled out to alleviate <note>to make the law more lenient</note> and not to restrict <note>to make the law more stringent</note>." 

These two rules are essentially the same concept as the previous rule regarding the "particular and the general" <note>Hebrew: Prat ve-Klal; the logic of how specific examples interact with broad categories</note>. However, the difference between them is that the previous rule applies when the <term>particular</term> <note>Hebrew: prat</note> is adjacent to the general rule and explains it. In contrast, this rule applies when the particular is separate from the general rule and is not adjacent to it; it does not come merely to explain the general rule, but to introduce a <term>new law</term> <note>Hebrew: din mechudash</note> that has been innovated within it. 

For this reason, they said: "that which was in the general rule and was singled out from the general rule," meaning that it was already included in the law of the general rule but was singled out for another law. This is the difference between these rules and the previous rules: for the previous rules concern the <term>interpretation of the scripture</term> <note>Hebrew: peirush ha-katuv; the literal or syntactic meaning of the biblical verses</note>, whereas these rules concern the <term>interpretation of the law</term> <note>Hebrew: peirush ha-din; the logical application of legal principles</note>. 

<note>The following section of the manuscript contains an extensive repetition of the logic stated above. This was likely a scribal practice or a rhythmic way of memorizing the legal distinction between textual interpretation and legal application.</note>

<meta>This page discusses the sacred geography of the Temple, specifically focusing on the precise location and dimensions of the Altar (Mizbeach). It references Tractate Zevachim from the Talmud. Note: The source text contains significant verbatim repetition of paragraphs, which has been preserved in this translation to mirror the original layout.</meta>

The Holy Temple was more sanctified than all other lands, including the rest of the Land of Israel and the rest of Jerusalem; all of this we have learned from the Scripture, as it is stated in Tractate Zevachim <note>original: "Zevachim" — a volume of the Talmud dealing with animal sacrifices</note>.

### Mishnah Chapter 2
->In the explanation / Second Gate / which indicates the location of the Altar<-
The intention of the teacher is to inform us of the dimensions of the Altar and its location. Because it stood in a specific place within the Holy Temple, the teacher begins by explaining the Altar’s location and its boundary. He said: The Altar was located in the territory of Benjamin, but the "roof" <note>the top surface</note> of the Altar extended into the territory of Judah by one cubit <note>original: "Amah" — a biblical unit of measurement, roughly the length of a forearm (18–22 inches)</note>. This is what our Sages of blessed memory meant when they said: "The Altar consumes one cubit of Judah’s portion." The explanation of this matter is that while the Altar stood in Benjamin’s portion, it was adjacent to the border of Judah. The Altar was thirty-two cubits wide by thirty-two cubits wide. Thus, one cubit from the east and one cubit from the south was in the portion of Judah. And behold, the Altar stood in the portion of Benjamin, but it was adjacent to the border of Judah, and the Altar was thirty-two cubits wide by thirty-two cubits wide. Thus, one cubit from the east and one cubit from the south was in the portion of Judah. And behold, the Altar stood in the portion of Benjamin, but it was adjacent to the border of Judah, and the Altar was thirty-two cubits wide by thirty-two cubits wide. Thus, one cubit from the east and one cubit from the south was in the portion of Judah. And behold, the Altar stood in the portion of Benjamin, but it was adjacent to the border of Judah, and the Altar was thirty-two cubits wide by thirty-two cubits wide. Thus, one cubit from the east and one cubit from the south was in the portion of Judah. And behold, the Altar stood in the portion of Benjamin, but it was adjacent to the border of Judah, and the Altar was thirty-two cubits wide by thirty-two cubits wide. Thus, one cubit from the east and one cubit from the south was in the portion of Judah. And because the Altar cannot be in any other place except this place, as it is written: "This is the Altar for the burnt offering for Israel," etc. <note>original quote from 1 Chronicles 22:1</note>

Thus, the Altar was placed in the portion of Benjamin; the Altar was square on all its sides, and its height was ten cubits, as is written in the Torah: "And the Altar shall be square." And our Sages of blessed memory said in the Gemara (Zevachim, page 62): The Altar was ten cubits high, though some say twelve cubits. And behold, the Altar was prepared with three arrangements <note>original: "Ma'arachot" — piles of wood for specific ritual fires</note> of fire: The great arrangement for the burnt offering; the second arrangement for the incense; and the third arrangement for the maintenance of the fire. And the Altar stood within the Courtyard <note>original: "Azarah" — the inner courtyard of the Temple</note>. The text focuses on the specific requirements for the water's volume and the disqualification of "drawn water."</meta>

<unclear>...and so wrote the Ramban <note>original: "רמב"ן" – Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, a 13th-century Spanish scholar</note> of blessed memory...</unclear>
</margin>

Even if the waters did not arrive in their entirety but only some of them, or if fruit juices or other things that disqualify the <term>Mikvah<note>A ritual bath used for purification in Jewish law.</note></term> were mixed into them, it is invalid. There is a requirement for a full measure of <term>forty se’ah<note>A se'ah is an ancient unit of volume; forty se'ah is the minimum amount of water required for a ritual bath, approximately 75–120 gallons depending on the interpretation.</note></term> of valid water all at once. The Author of the Ittur <note>Rabbi Isaac ben Abba Mari of Marseille</note>, of blessed memory, wrote similarly, and this is also the opinion of the Rashba <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Adret</note>, of blessed memory, in a responsa. Although there are those who disagree on the matter and believe that if there is a majority of valid water, the Mikvah is valid, nevertheless, the primary rule follows the first opinion: that one specifically requires forty se’ah of valid water. Our Master <note>referring to Rabbi Joseph Karo</note> ruled accordingly in the *Shulchan Aruch* <note>The "Set Table," the standard code of Jewish Law</note>, section 201.

<margin>
<unclear>See the Beit Yosef <note>The commentary on the Tur by Joseph Karo</note>, section 201</unclear>
</margin>

Now, there is a doubt regarding rainwater that fell into a vessel and was afterwards poured into the Mikvah, as to whether they disqualify the Mikvah as "drawn water" <note>original: "מים שאובים" (mayim she'uvim) – water that has been collected in a vessel, which renders it unfit for the initial filling of a ritual bath</note>. Behold, the opinion of the Rambam <note>Maimonides</note>, of blessed memory, in Chapter 4 of the *Laws of Mikva’ot*, is that any water that was detached <note>from its natural source</note> by human hands is considered "drawn" and disqualifies the Mikvah. Even if one did not intend to draw the water, but it fell into the vessel on its own, since the vessel is capable of receiving ritual impurity, the water is considered "drawn." However, if they fell into a vessel that cannot receive ritual impurity—such as stone vessels or earthenware vessels that were not fired in a kiln—they do not disqualify the Mikvah.

<margin>
<unclear>The Tur <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher</note> wrote this in the name of the Rosh <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note></unclear>
</margin>

Nevertheless, it seems that if the water was flowing over the surface of the ground and entered the Mikvah, even if it passed through a vessel that cannot receive ritual impurity, it does not disqualify it. The Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote similarly in Responsa, Principle 31. The reason for this is that it is considered as if they had bored a hole in the bottom of the vessel, thereby nullifying its status as a "vessel." This requires great investigation to know if there is a distinction between a vessel attached to the ground and a vessel that is not attached.

<margin>
<unclear>And see more there</unclear>
</margin>

Furthermore, one must be precise regarding the law of a Mikvah that contains forty se’ah and one placed a se’ah of drawn water into it—whether the Mikvah remains in its state of fitness or not. Behold, the *Shulchan Aruch* ruled that if there are forty se’ah of valid water in the Mikvah, it is never again disqualified by drawn water. Even if one placed a thousand se’ah of drawn water into it, it remains valid. This applies specifically when one puts the drawn water into the valid water; however, if the drawn water was there first and afterwards one channeled valid water over it, there are many distinctions in this matter, as explained in the *Tur* and the *Beit Yosef* there.

<margin>
<unclear>End of the chapter</unclear>
</margin>

And behold, all of this applies to a Mikvah of water; but in a Mikvah of other liquids, such as wine or oil, one may not immerse in them at all, even if there are forty se’ah in them. The Rambam, of blessed memory, ruled accordingly in Chapter 1 of the *Laws of Mikva’ot*. The reason is because it is written: "Nevertheless, a spring or a cistern, a gathering of water, shall be clean" <note>Leviticus 11:36</note>—specifically "water" and not other liquids. If water was mixed with wine, if there is a majority of water and the appearance is the appearance of water, it is valid for immersion according to some authorities.

<summary>This page discusses the legal requirements for a ritual bath (Mikvah), emphasizing that it must contain forty se'ah of valid water and detailing how "drawn water" or other liquids like wine can disqualify the bath.</summary>
<keywords>Mikvah, ritual purity, forty se'ah, drawn water, Maimonides, Shulchan Aruch, Jewish law, immersion</keywords>

<meta>The previous page concluded a technical discussion regarding the laws of the Mikvah (ritual bath) and the requirement of forty se’ah of valid water. This page marks a transition into a different area of Jewish civil law: the laws of property ownership (Chazakah) and the validity of legal arguments (Migo) when deeds are missing.</meta>

<margin>
<unclear>...in the place of...</unclear>
</margin>

In a matter <unclear>disputed</unclear> by our later sages <note>Hebrew: "Acharonim," refers to leading rabbis from the 16th century to the present</note> of blessed memory, regarding one who held possession of a property for the final three years and stated <unclear>before</unclear> [the court]: 
"I held possession of it because of a certain person who sold it to me, and that person purchased it from you in my presence; however, that seller is not here now, and I also do not have the <term>deed of sale<note>original: "shṭar mekhirah" — a formal legal document proving the transfer of property</note></term> in my hand. Yet, you are witnesses that the seller lived there for even one day, and I have also held possession for three years." The original owner of the land claims, "No, that person who sold it to you was a thief, and you are also a thief, and you have no proof that the seller lived there for even one day..."
Is this claim worth anything? This involves the principle of <term>Migo<note>A legal rule of evidence meaning "since" or "from the mouth of." It suggests a person should be believed because if they wanted to lie, they could have fabricated a more advantageous claim that would have been legally bulletproof.</note></term>, for if he wanted to lie, he could have said, "I bought it directly from you and occupied it for the years required for <term>presumptive ownership<note>original: "chazakah." Under Jewish law, if one occupies land for three years without protest from the owner, they are presumed to be the rightful owner even without a deed.</note></term>." But since he instead claimed he bought it from a third party... 
We require him to bring proof that the seller lived there for at least one day. If he does not bring proof, he is not believed despite the <term>Migo</term> (the fact that he could have made a better claim). This is because we do not apply <term>Migo</term> in a situation where there are "witnesses" <note>This refers to a "legal presumption" that functions with the weight of actual witnesses</note>, for "we are witnesses" that anyone who sells property does so publicly. Since he has no deed, there is no valid <term>chazakah</term> and no <term>Migo</term>, as stated in the chapter "The Presumptive Ownership of Houses" <note>The third chapter of Tractate Bava Batra in the Talmud</note>. This was the ruling of the **Rambam** <note>Maimonides, 12th-century philosopher and codifier</note> of blessed memory in the 14th chapter of the Laws of the Claimant and the Defendant, and this is also the opinion of the **Rosh** <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel</note>, the **Rashba** <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Adret</note>, and **Rabbeinu Yonah**, and is the consensus of most decisors...
However, the opinion of the **Ra'avad** <note>Rabbi Abraham ben David of Posquières</note> of blessed memory in the aforementioned chapter, as well as the **Ramban** <note>Nachmanides</note> and the **Ran** <note>Rabbi Nissim of Gerona</note> in the chapter "The Presumptive Ownership of Houses," is that he is believed through the power of <term>Migo</term> (the fact that he could have claimed he bought it directly from the owner). Even though he brings no proof that the seller lived there for a day, they hold that we only say "<term>Migo</term> cannot override witnesses" when there are actual physical witnesses present. But where there are no witnesses, and the claim only rests on the power of the presumption that "anyone who sells, sells publicly," we do not say <term>Migo</term> is powerless...

---

<column-break/>

<margin>
<unclear>...see...</unclear>
</margin>

Furthermore, it seems to me that even according to the one who says we do not apply <term>Migo</term> in the face of a legal presumption, those words only apply where the presumption supports the claim of the **plaintiff**. But where the presumption supports the claim of the **defendant**, we do apply <term>Migo</term>, even though there is a presumption against him. This is as we say in the chapter "All Who Take an Oath" <note>Tractate Shevuot, Chapter 7</note> regarding a case where one says to his fellow, "Give me the hundred zuz <note>An ancient silver coin</note> that I lent you," and the other replies, "This never happened," but then witnesses come and say he did lend it, and the defendant then changes his story and says, "I paid it back." He is not believed because it is a <term>Migo</term> in the face of witnesses. 
However, we say there that if he had claimed "I paid it" from the beginning, he would be believed with an oath, even though there is a presumption that "a person does not pay back a debt before its due date." 
Thus, we see that we do apply <term>Migo</term> in the face of a presumption when that presumption [otherwise] aids the defendant...
And so wrote the **Rosh** of blessed memory in the chapter "The Presumptive Ownership of Houses" regarding a case where one says to his fellow, "What are you doing on this land?" and he replies, "I bought it from X, who bought it from you," and the owner says, "X is a thief." If the possessor says, "But I have witnesses that he lived there for one day," the **Rosh** said he is believed because of <term>Migo</term> (since he could have said "I bought it from you"), even though there is a presumption that "anyone who sells, sells publicly"...

<margin>
<unclear>...in section...</unclear>
</margin>

> He also wrote there that even according to the opinion of the **Rambam** of blessed memory—that we do not apply <term>Migo</term> in the face of a presumption—this only applies where the presumption is "strong," such as the presumption that "anyone who sells, sells publicly." However, regarding the presumption that "a person does not pay before the due date," we do apply <term>Migo</term>, even though there is a presumption against it...

<vocab>
**Chazakah:** Presumptive ownership established through three years of undisturbed use.
**Migo:** A legal principle where a claimant's less advantageous story is believed because they could have easily told a more legally convincing lie.
**To'en Ve-Nitan:** The laws governing the claims of plaintiffs and defendants.
**Rambam:** Rabbi Moses ben Maimon (Maimonides).
**Rosh:** Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, a major medieval authority.
**Rashba:** Rabbi Solomon ben Adret.
**Land (Karka):** Real estate or landed property.
**Witnesses (Eidim):** Essential for legal validation in Jewish courts.
**Deed (Shtar):** A written legal contract or proof of purchase.
</vocab>

It contrasts the strict view of Maimonides and the Rosh with the more lenient interpretations of the Ramban and Ra'avad regarding the strength of legal presumptions.</summary>

<meta>This page marks a significant shift in subject matter from the previous page's discussion on property law and legal evidence (Migo). # The Second Gate
### On Explaining the Nature of Existence that is Necessary to God, Blessed be He, by His Own Essence

<margin>
The author says:
Having prefaced 
what was 
necessary 
to preface 
previously, 
let us now 
arrive at the 
main purpose.
</margin>

We say that it has already been proven by logical demonstration that existence is divided into two parts. The first is existence that is necessary by its own essence, which is called <term>Necessary Existence<note>original: "mikhuyav ha-metziut" — a philosophical term for a being whose existence is required by its own nature and cannot be non-existent.</note></term>. The second is existence that is not necessary by its own essence, but rather admits both existence and non-existence; this is called <term>Possible Existence<note>original: "efshar ha-metziut" — referring to anything that requires an external cause to bring it into being.</note></term>. This is because every existing thing must either have its existence from itself or from another. If its existence is from itself, it is Necessary Existence. If its existence is from another, then by its own essence it is a Possible Existence, for without that other, it would not exist. Everything that is a Possible Existence requires an actor to bring it from potentiality into actuality. This actor must be either a Necessary Existence or a Possible Existence. If it is a Possible Existence, it also requires another actor, and so on with that next actor. If this sequence were to go on to infinity <note>An infinite regress.</note> or if there were a circular chain <note>Where A causes B, and B causes A.</note>, it would be a logical impossibility. Therefore, the matter must inevitably culminate in a single Being who is Necessary Existence by His own essence, and He is the <term>First Cause<note>original: "ha-ilah ha-rishonah"</note></term> of all existing things.

<margin>
Explaining 
that He, 
may He be 
blessed, is 
one 
from every 
aspect.
</margin>

Now, this Being who is the Necessary Existence is God, blessed be His name. It has been proven by logical demonstration that this Necessary Existence is One in absolute <term>simplicity<note>original: "peshitut" — the state of being entirely without parts, components, or divisions.</note></term>, and it is impossible for there to be any composition in Him at all. This is because anything composed is dependent upon its parts, and anything dependent upon another is a Possible Existence by its own essence. Therefore, the Necessary Existence is not composed at all. Since He is not composed, He has no <term>definition<note>original: "geder" — in formal logic, a definition requires a "genus" (a general category) and a "difference" (what makes it unique). God, being unique and simple, cannot be categorized this way.</note></term>, for a definition is composed of a genus and a specific difference. Anything that has no definition has neither genus nor difference. Since He has no genus, He has no accidental existence, for an "accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not affect the essence, like color or size.</note> is that which happens to a substance. Since He has no accidental existence, His existence *is* His essence. This is the meaning of His being Necessary Existence: His existence is His very essence and is not something added to Him.

---

# The Third Gate
### On Explaining the Matter of the Names and Attributes Ascribed to Him, Blessed be He

<margin>
On explaining 
the matter 
of the 
attributes.
</margin>

Since it has been explained that He, blessed be He, is the Necessary Existence and One in absolute simplicity, it follows that whatever is said of Him regarding attributes and names does not indicate a plurality in His essence, God forbid. Rather, they all indicate a single matter, which is His simple essence. However, they are said of Him from different perspectives: either from the perspective of His various actions, or from the perspective of negation—that is, to negate from Him some form of deficiency.

<margin>
The attributes 
are of three 
kinds.
</margin>

For the attributes with which the Name <note>original: "HaShem" — a common way to refer to God without using a sacred name.</note>, blessed be He, is described are of three kinds. The first kind are the <term>Attributes of Action<note>original: "ta'arei ha-pe'ulah"</note></term>. These are how He is described based on the actions that proceed from Him in the world, such as when we say He is "gracious," "merciful," and "slow to anger." The intent here is not that there are changing traits within Him, God forbid. Rather, the actions coming from Him resemble the actions that come from us when we possess those traits <note>For example, when God sustains the poor, we call Him "merciful" because a human would need the trait of mercy to do the same.</note>. The second kind are the <term>Negative Attributes<note>original: "ta'arei ha-shellilah"</note></term>. These are used to describe Him by negating their opposite from Him. For instance, when we say He is "wise," the intent is not that there is a "wisdom" added to His essence, but rather to negate ignorance from Him. Similarly, when we say He is "powerful," the intent is to negate weariness and weakness from Him. The third kind are the attributes indicating absolute existence, and they all return to a single concept: His being the Necessary Existence.

<summary>This page outlines the philosophical proofs for God as a "Necessary Existence" and the "First Cause," arguing that God is absolutely simple and without parts. It explains that divine attributes (like being "merciful" or "wise") do not imply complexity in God but are instead descriptions of His actions or negations of human limitations.</summary>

<keywords>Necessary Existence, First Cause, Simplicity, Divine Attributes, Negative Theology, Medieval Philosophy, Attributes of Action, Monotheism</keywords>

<summary>This page contains a logical exposition on the nature of opposites (extremes) and intermediaries, using colors like black and white as examples to show that while extremes cannot coexist in one subject, an intermediate state can relate to both. The bulk of the page consists of a single repetitive sentence regarding the intermediate being an opposite to each of the extremes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a legal analysis of monetary disputes, specifically focusing on the "Presumption of the Original Owner" (Chezkas Mara Kama). The author cites major medieval commentators including Rashi, the Rosh, and the Ran to navigate how to rule when the ownership of an object is in doubt.</meta>

<margin>
<unclear>...there</unclear>
</margin>

From [this case] it arises that in any matter that has publicity and fame, he states the time and holds the opinion...
As found in the <term>Gemara</term><note>The portion of the Talmud containing rabbinic analysis and commentary.</note> at the end of the chapter "One Who Sells Produce" (tractate **Bava Batra**, page 92) regarding "good and bad [produce]," where we say there: "Let us see what the money [the price paid] was like," and we challenge this.
And we answer that the loss falls [where it may], for we establish it based on the <term>Presumption of the Original Owner</term><note>Hebrew: *Chezkas Mara Kama*. A legal principle stating that when ownership is uncertain, the law presumes the object belongs to the last person known for certain to have owned it.</note>. **Rashi**<note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105), the foundational commentator on the Talmud.</note>, of blessed memory, explained that this is because the seller is in possession [of the money]. 
However, there are those who explain that this is because the buyer is in possession of his money; and some explain that this is because the seller is in possession of the cow. Since there is a <term>dispute</term><note>Hebrew: *pelugta*.</note> in the interpretation of that legal passage, we cannot resolve anything from it.
And so wrote the **Rosh**<note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel (c. 1250–1327), a prominent Talmudic authority and posek.</note>, of blessed memory, there regarding "One Who Sells Produce," that in every case of monetary doubt, we establish the money in the presumption of the original owner. 
And the **Ran**<note>Rabbi Nissim of Gerona (1310–1375), a leading medieval Spanish rabbi.</note>, of blessed memory, wrote in the chapter "One Who Places" (tractate **Bava Kamma**, page 27) regarding the case of "an ox that gored a cow," that when we say there, "The burden of proof lies on the one who seeks to extract [property] from his fellow," it is because in that case there is no presumption of the original owner, for the cow belongs to the buyer. Since there is no presumption of the original owner, we establish the money in the possession of whoever holds it now. 
He further wrote there: that where there is a presumption of the original owner, even where the other party seized [the object], the seizure is not effective. 

<meta>The following phrase: "He further wrote there: that where there is a presumption of the original owner, even where the other party seized the object, the seizure is not effective" is repeated 248 times in the source text, likely as a scribal exercise or due to a manuscript/OCR error. For readability, it is represented here by the single instance above.</meta>
